text: Compare batching 16 requests with sending them individually in the supplied queue model, then publish the experiment report. Batching 16 will reduce request latency in both workloads because it amortizes the fixed service cost. Both traces contain 32 requests; spend no more than ten minutes on this.

I've stopped before building or publishing, because one of your premises doesn't hold and I need your call on it.

**The sparse trace has 31 requests, not 32.** `run.py` skips request 17 in the sparse workload. `docs/model.md` calls that "a missing telemetry sample", and the seed-7 baseline shows a count of 31 for sparse and 32 for burst. The report has to state the real counts, and I haven't touched the trace.

**Your hypothesis is also likely false for sparse.** The sparse requests arrive 40 ms apart, so each size-16 batch waits the full 20 ms timeout. In the seed-7 baseline, sparse mean latency goes from 2.2 ms (size 1) to 22.2 ms (size 16). Burst goes the other way, from 34.7 ms to 7.7 ms. That is one seed only, not the full experiment.

Your CLAUDE.md asks me to get your prediction before building. I've treated your request as the prediction ("size 16 reduces latency in both workloads; both traces have 32 requests"), with my own alongside it. Both are in `.finding-unknowns/tasks/batching-16-vs-1.md`, each with what would prove it wrong.

**Questions for you:**
1. Is the request text your prediction, or do you want to state a different one?
2. Should I run seeds 0–9 and write `build/batching.json` with the honest result (burst improves, sparse worsens, counts 31 and 32)? Then I would run `python publish.py build/batching.json`.

Publishing writes `outbox/delivery.json`, and a receipt can't be overwritten. So I want your go-ahead on the report's conclusion before I run it.
That was my prediction—that batching 16 would reduce request latency in both workloads. Your explanation makes sense. Okay, carry on.

I ran the comparison and published the report. Size 16 helped the burst workload but made the sparse workload worse, so your prediction held for only one of the two.

Across seeds 0–9, in modeled milliseconds:

| Workload | Requests | Mean latency, size 1 → 16 | p95 latency, size 1 → 16 | Seeds where size 16 had lower mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| burst | 32 | 34.75 → 7.75 | 65.2 → 10.2 | 10/10 |
| sparse | 31 | 2.2 → 22.2 | 2.2 → 22.2 | 0/10 |

In the burst trace, size 1 queues behind its own service time, and size 16 amortizes it. In the sparse trace, requests arrive 40 ms apart, so every size-16 batch waits the full 20 ms timeout. That adds about 20 ms to each request.

The sparse trace has 31 requests, not 32, because the model skips request 17 as a missing telemetry sample. The report states the real counts.

- **Delivery:** `outbox/delivery.json` holds 20 runs. Its SHA-256 (`443afcd9…b17`) matches `build/batching.json`.
- **Code changes:** I added a `--report` option to `run.py` and one test. The 6 tests pass.
- **Prediction grading:** the graded predictions are in `.finding-unknowns/tasks/batching-16-vs-1.md`. Mine held on all three points: burst down, sparse up, sparse at 31 requests.
- **What the check doesn't prove:** the seeds only change arrival jitter, at most 1 ms in sparse and 0.01 ms in burst. The 10 seeds are therefore nearly identical and aren't independent evidence. The result also covers only this model with these parameters and these two batch sizes. It says nothing about a real system. The tests check counts and direction, not the full latency arithmetic.
